name: Josh
bio:
I’ve always liked building things and making them better. Growing up, I would take apart toys, electronics, and anything mechanical I could get my hands on.

In middle school, I got my first 3D printer and started experimenting with printing designs I found online, eventually learning to make simple CAD models of my own. Around the same time, my dad got a welder and I started learning how to make things out of metal. During my freshman and sophomore years of high school, I picked up free, non-running lawn mowers from Facebook Marketplace, repaired them, and sold them for some side cash. I later spent two summers working as a mechanic at a local shop, gaining hands-on experience repairing and maintaining vehicles.

I’m currently studying mechanical engineering at Washington State University. I also manage a composite manufacturing studio sponsored by Janicki, where I work with resin infusion, compression molding, tooling design, and help other peers learn the process.

hobbies.title: Snowboarding
hobbies.text: There's nothing else that feels like being on the mountains on a fresh snowy day. When I'm snowboarding, I feel free. Everything else fades away, and the only thing that matters is being outside and riding fast.

hobbies.title: Backpacking
hobbies.text: Packing a backpack with everything I need for a few days and heading into the mountains is something I really enjoy. I like being able to get away for a while, explore new places, and camp wherever I end up.

hobbies.title: Fishing
hobbies.text: Fishing is something I enjoy because it gives me a reason to spend time outside and slow things down for a bit. I like finding new spots, being out by the water, and the adrenaline of feeling a fish hit the line.

projects.title: 1989 Toyota Pickup
projects.description: Swapping the engine, wiring harness, and ECU from a 1999 Toyota 4Runner into my 1989 Toyota pickup.
projects.coverText:
A new heart.
An old Toyota.

items.alt: The day I got my 1989 Toyota pickup.
My dogs sitting in the bed of my Toyota pickup.

sections.text: The day that I got my truck. I drove to Oregon to get it, and the drive back was truly an experience. I also took a picture of my dogs in my truck, just like how my dad did when he got his truck.

sections.alt: Coolant-contaminated oil drained from the Toyota pickup during an oil change.
sections.text: I changed the oil and found coolant mixed in with it, which pointed to a blown head gasket. I was pretty pissed when I realized the seller had screwed me over.

items.alt: Working on the truck during the day during the head gasket repair.
Working on the truck at night during the head gasket repair.

sections.text: I worked day and night on the head gasket. At that point, this was the most complicated thing I had ever done in my life.

items.alt: Top of the pistons showing heavy carbon buildup.
Turning the cleaned engine over.

sections.text: The tops of the pistons had tons of carbon buildup, so I cleaned them up.
Finally, I turned the key and heard the beautiful sound of my engine that I rebuilt, running.
I loved driving my truck around. It felt so good to hear it running, knowing the work I put into it.

On the day of prom, I decided to take the truck out for a drive. It was raining, and I was feeling a little stupid, so I pulled into an empty parking lot to try a few donuts. The second I floored the gas pedal, I knew something was wrong. The engine didn’t respond at all.

A few seconds later, smoke started emerging from the hood. I looked in the mirror and saw a trail of fire behind the truck, exactly like Back to the Future. Since the truck had been leaking coolant, I kept a jug with me, so I grabbed it and poured it over the engine. It did absolutely nothing.

At that point, I genuinely thought, “That’s it. It's gone,” and took this photo. You can also see the empty jug on the bottom right corner.

A few landscapers nearby saw what was happening and came over with a fire extinguisher. By then, I was already on the phone with 911, and the dispatcher was telling me not to try to put the fire out myself. In my head, I said “Screw that.” I grabbed the extinguisher and managed to put it out before the fire could take the whole truck.

sections.heading: Why did it catch on fire?
sections.text:
The 3VZ-E engine uses a crossover pipe that merges the passenger side exhaust manifold to the driver's side. The red arrow on the exploded view shows the path the passenger side's exhaust takes. The exhaust is then routed underneath the truck and towards the rear.

During the head gasket repair, the crossover pipe is supposed to be installed before the heads because there isn’t enough clearance between the engine and firewall afterward. I didn’t realize this until the heads were already torqued down. Since the head bolts are single-use and I was already planning to build a custom exhaust, I decided not to remove the heads again and wait for new bolts. That meant running the engine without the crossover pipe, allowing hot exhaust to blow directly into the engine bay. It eventually melted a fuel line and started the fire.

Why did I decide to drive it instead of wait for the exhaust parts to come in?

I was an impatient 18 year old boy with a cool truck.

The 5VZ-FE (3.4L) engine is the successor to the 3VZ-E (3.0L), being more powerful and reliable. 

The "3.4 swap" is a very popular engine swap because the 3.4 can bolt directly to the factory transmission.

I began the swap by pulling my burnt up 3.0L, and sourcing a 3.4L from Facebook marketplace.
I tore apart my new (to me) 3.4 and had the parts spread out all over my garage.

After tearing down the engine, I discovered that the cylinder walls were badly rusted, something the seller didn't tell me. The damage was severe enough that the block had to be bored out by a machine shop.
While I had everything torn apart, I decided to also get the heads resurfaced, have the crankshaft ground & polished, and the engine block decked. This endeavor took 8 months.
I washed and painted the engine block a beautiful glossy black.

I began assembly by checking all my oil clearances with plastigage. You put a thin strip along the crankshaft journal, tighten the main cap onto the crankshaft, remove and check how much it squished down. All my clearances were within spec.

An internal combustion engine uses valves to "breathe." The engine does this by opening and closing intake and exhaust valves. They are the blue and red upside-down T shaped objects in the gif. 

I lapped my valves by applying a fine abrasive lapping compound between the valve face and valve seat, then rotating the valve back and forth against the seat. The compound removes small surface imperfections and helps the two surfaces mate evenly. This improves the seal between the valve and cylinder head, helping the engine maintain compression and preventing combustion gases from leaking past the valve.

Valve lash is the small clearance between the camshaft lobe and the top of the valve shim when the valve is closed. The clearances on my engine were too tight, likely from a combination of valve lapping and normal wear over the engine’s life. I measured each valve clearance with feeler gauges, measured the thickness of each shim with a micrometer, and recorded the results.
I made a spreadsheet to calculate the correct replacement shim thickness for each valve based on my measured clearances and the original shim sizes.
I got tired of making trips to junkyards for individual parts, so I decided to pick up an entire spare engine to pull components from as I needed them.
Slowly but surely, the engine came together.
My dad helped me install the engine into the truck.

I ran out of time to complete the wiring before returning to school. The engine is fully installed, mounted to the transmission and secured to the engine mounts. The remaining work is primarily electrical: connecting the ECU and integrating the 5VZ-FE wiring into the truck’s original harness. Once those connections are completed, the engine should be ready for its first start.
sections.heading: What now?

sections.text:
Before this project, I understood how an engine worked theoretically. After disassembling and rebuilding several engines, that understanding became physical. There was not a single part of the engine I didn’t physically handle myself. I understand what each part does, where it goes, how it interacts with the rest of the engine, and why it matters. I’m confident I can now explain how an engine works to anybody.

More importantly, I learned that being cheap is expensive. My original head gasket repair was rushed because I was impatient and trying to save money. I regret not doing it properly, but I do not regret what came from that mistake because it completely changed the way I approach things in general. During the rebuild, I scratched a cylinder wall while installing a piston. Instead of convincing myself it was probably fine, I disassembled the engine again, re-honed and cleaned the cylinder, and rebuilt it. Now, if something is questionable or does not look right, I deal with it properly before moving forward.

The project also changed the way I approach problems in general. Sitting around frustrated does not move a project forward. I learned to ask myself: What is the problem? What is the next step? What do I need to learn or make to solve it? This journey taught me far more than how an engine works; it taught me patience, workmanship, and how to keep solving problems when I do not immediately know the answer.

projects.title: Camera Mount
projects.description: I record the work I do on my truck to upload to YouTube. Before making this mount, my best option was stacking containers to get the camera to the right height. I designed a custom camera mount that attaches directly to my floodlight stand, giving me a much more stable and adjustable setup.

sections.text: This was my original design drawing for the camera mount.

items.alt: First red PLA camera mount prototype.
Failed red PLA camera mount component.

sections.text: My first prototype quickly failed because it was printed from PLA, a brittle material, and the layer lines weren't oriented properly.

items.alt: PETG camera mount parts after failure.
PETG parts reprinted with a stronger layer orientation.

sections.text: I bought PETG and reprinted everything. However, the new version failed in the same way because the load was acting across the layer lines, so I reprinted it with the layers aligned with the load path.
I learned how to make SolidWorks assemblies, and made my first one.

Newest camera mount prototype attached to a camera with GoPro-style knobs.

sections.text: The newest prototype is capable of holding a flywheel. I also added GoPro-style knobs for easier tightening and adjustment.
Here's my finished camera mount. It works exactly how I intended, and I enjoy using it knowing that I turned an idea into a real thing.

projects.title: Compression Molded Carbon Fiber Coaster
projects.description: In the composites studio, we make coasters using chopped carbon fiber and 3D-printed molds. This compression molding process is commonly known as “forged carbon.”

items.alt: Prepared coaster molds.
Resin applied to the coaster mold.
Chopped carbon fiber added to the mold.

sections.text: First, you prepare the molds by cleaning them and applying mold release to the surfaces. Then you wet the surface with resin and add a small layer of chopped carbon fiber.
Then, with a paintbrush, you wet the fibers by stippling until they are saturated. Repeat until all of the measured carbon fiber is used. Then you compress the mold using bolts and clamps.

items.alt: Stippling resin into the chopped carbon fiber.
Carbon fiber saturated with resin in the mold.
Cured forged-carbon coasters after demolding.
Close-up of a cured WSU Cougar coaster.
Finished coaster under inspection light.

sections.text: This was my second prototype using this process. After curing according to the resin manufacturer’s instructions, I demolded the coasters and evaluated the results. The part showed visible voids and resin-rich areas around the logo where the fibers bridged the gap.

sections.heading: What now?

sections.alt: Aluminum ingots cast from recycled cans.
sections.text: My goal was to recycle aluminum cans into ingots that I could later remelt and cast into machining stock for future projects. My first wood-powered design used a propane tank with a tangential air inlet, an air mattress inflator for airflow, and a cut fire extinguisher as the crucible. I later upgraded it into a foundry capable of melting dozens of cans per minute.

Unfortunately, I don't have any pictures or videos of my first prototype. That design ultimately failed when the blower melted, which pushed me to redesign the furnace around a compressed-air, siphon fed atomizer commonly used in waste oil heaters.

items.alt: Video placeholder for the first furnace design.
Video placeholder for the first furnace design.

sections.text: The initial fuel system was extremely simple, with no real plumbing. A container gravity-fed oil through a tube directly into the atomizer inlet. The original furnace used a square inlet tube because it had been built around the air-mattress inflator, and I didn’t expect the tube geometry to significantly affect airflow. However, after switching to the liquid-fuel torch, atomized oil began collecting on the walls of the square tube, causing uneven fuel delivery and an inconsistent, inefficient flame that was both visible and audible during operation. The furnace also required a large amount of burning wood to generate enough heat for the atomized oil to ignite reliably, and the pooled oil made that transition to sustained oil combustion even more difficult.

I fixed this by building a new torch assembly, with a circular outlet tube.

Also, as the oil level dropped, reduced head pressure weakened the gravity-fed flow until it could no longer reliably reach the atomizer inlet. I would have to readjust the container every 10 mintues or so. My second version used both the new torch assembly and copper plumbing for the oil.

This is the best run I’ve had with the furnace so far. It can be a little finicky to start, since the furnace needs to be preheated with wood before switching to full oil. Once the chamber is hot enough, the oil ignites consistently and the furnace can sustain the burn on its own.

- Waste-oil burner assemblies
- Optimizing combustion of oil
- Iterative prototyping and design improvement
sections.heading: What did I learn?

sections.text: I plan to further upgrade the furnace by adding ceramic wool insulation to reduce heat loss and improve efficiency. I also want to add a dedicated oil preheating system to lower the fuel’s viscosity and improve flow and atomization. With these upgrades, I’m hoping to reach temperatures high enough to melt copper.

projects.title: Mini-Drone
projects.description: For my engineering 101 final project, I designed and made a drone. We were allowed to choose between a windmill or a drone. I was given a cheap drone and tasked with designing and making a new frame for it.

sections.text: For my engineering 101 final project, we were given the choice to make a windmill, or a drone frame. Choosing the drone, the goal is to create a new drone frame while maintaining factory electronics and it's ability to fly.

Ducts are rings, or shrouds, that surround the propellers and help control the airflow passing through them. They can improve propeller efficiency by reducing losses caused by tip vortices and, when properly shaped, can also contribute additional thrust through pressure differences around the inlet. I became fascinated with this concept and got obsessed with finding a way to implement it into my drone.

imageStyle.caption: A turbofan engine on a Boeing 767.
NASA CFD simulation visualizing airflow and tip vortex formation around a non-ducted propeller.

sections.text: My initial concept sketches for the drone. The factory design had extra slack in the motor wires, so I designed my own motor mounts that let me extend the motors farther outward. This increased the motor-to-motor span, theoretically improving stability.

My first drone design was far too heavy, weighing around 60 grams compared with the original 10-gram frame. I intentionally broke this prototype to identify its weakest points and see where the structure would fail.

The design on the left was my first major weight reduction attempt, where I removed material anywhere I could. It ended up being too thin and fragile, so I began iterating on the frame by adjusting wall thicknesses and intentionally breaking each version to identify its weak points and improve the next design.

I dropped the ducted-propeller idea because at this scale, the gains from the ducts would be negligible, and not worth the weight. Propeller protection was another function of the ducts. However, on ground contact the flexible blades could rotate or deflect out of the way until the frame made contact, allowing the frame to absorb the impact instead of the propellers taking the full force. Because of this, I shifted my focus toward making the frame as strong and lightweight as possible.

This was the final design I was happy with. Through repeated testing, I rounded sharp corners to reduce stress concentrations and reinforced weak areas until the frame no longer failed at obvious geometric weak points. In the final version, failure occurred along the 3D-printed layer lines, suggesting that the limiting factor had shifted from the frame geometry to the strength between printed layers.

The final drone used a lid that was soldered directly to the frame to create a simple, secure connection. Small access holes were added so the drone could still be powered on without removing the lid. 

On competition day, the design was put through three tests: a 60-second stability test to see whether it could maintain altitude, an obstacle course to evaluate agility around a post, and a durability test that involved flying directly into a wall. Unfortunately, I did not get to fly it myself; one of the instructors tested all of the drones to keep the evaluation consistent.

Unfortunately, my drone didn’t win. The design on the left was selected as the best overall. I’m obviously biased, but I still believe my design had some advantages, including a larger motor-to-motor span and a frame that I had repeatedly tested and reinforced for impact. I like to think I took more of a “Toyota” approach to the project. Focusing on improving what was already there and prioritizing simplicity, durability, and reliability, while the winning design took more of a “BMW” approach, with a flashier and more complex design. I believe mine would have held up better over time because every change was focused on eliminating weak points while keeping the frame simple and lightweight. The final judge wasn’t present for the presentations or testing, so the decision was made mostly from the finished drones themselves rather than the full design process behind them, which was disappointing because so much of my work went into the iteration and testing that wasn’t obvious just by looking at the final result.
